title: Scott Hall orchestrates Proclamation
summary: Conductor Scott Hall orchestrated Lewis's piano manuscript after working through it with him.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Once again I’d be amiss if I did not tell you about the name of the conductor, because I can’t recall it now. Can we stop here, or what? Kimery: Sure.

The conductor’s name is Scott Hall. Scott Hall not only conducted the piece, but he arranged and orchestrated the piece. I had in my head what I thought the sound could or would be, but he’s – because I wrote it at the piano – but he’s the one who took the music and orchestrated it.
How was that process? What was that process? You just handed him the piano score, and he just came back with the whole orchestration?

Yeah. I handed him the manuscript, but he also came over with a tape recorder – a digital recorder, and I sat at the piano and played and talked, like, here’s what I hear here, and this is what I hear here, and it seems like this should go well here if we do this. He took notes, and he listened to all that. It came out wonderfully well. We’re a good team.

The reason why I asked is because there are so many different processes of orchestration or arranging. For example, Gershwin – because we mentioned him perhaps off-mic – when he was writing Rhapsody in Blue, he’d write a segment and give it to Ferde Grofé, and he would orchestrate that. Then he’d write another section and give it to him. So it wasn’t a dialogue. It wasn’t this exchange.
Yeah. He wanted – Scott wanted to get it right. So not only did I give him the music, but we talked about it.
